top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B006) rewards one well-bounded mechanism. Collateral values and credit limits feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. It is about thirty years old, was tested in 2007-09, and is now part of the shared core of macro, finance and policy modelling. Its attribution is the least disputed on the slate. The two-name configuration avoids re-crediting the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator and the bank-run themes of the 2022 prize. I accept that direct identification of the specific collateral channel is mixed and that the proximity to 2022 is a real consideration. I rank P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) second because it is also compact and mature and has a stronger applied validation record. Its omissions (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard, Levin) are a real cost, and the margin over P003 is narrow. P002 over P001 would be a defensible weighting, and I prefer P001 only on breadth of conceptual influence. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is third. Its empirical designs are credible, but it bundles technology and trade strands, and its overlap with earlier prizes and the debate over shift-share inference weigh against it. No award is last because all three proposals describe mature, substantive achievements. These judgements rest on background knowledge and not on independently verified citation data.
recusal_note: Per my profile, I am a long-term co-author of John Hassler (chair, P001 supporter) and have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member, P003 supporter). I am an IIES colleague of both, and I am the committee secretary. My field of heterogeneous-agent macro is adjacent to B006. I am also a long-term co-author of Giovanni Violante (B043), which is not on the slate. None of Kiyotaki, Moore, Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes, Autor, Dorn or Hanson appears among my listed co-authors. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
